He said that he’s just busy with studying and all that stuff and I should give him space when he needs it. He also said that it was weird that I just showed up unannounced.

Scenario:
AITA for visiting my son unannounced. | My son’s(19) in an university. He’s in a different city and lives in an apartment with 2 of his friends. Ever since he left(2 months ago) he just started ignoring me. I didn’t call him excessively, maybe once in two days. He’d hang up or not answer and text me later that he’s busy. Few days ago I was in the city for unrelated reason. I called him because I wanted to visit him but he didn’t answer so I just went to the apartment. His friend answered the door, my son was sleeping. The apartment was filthy, empty bottles everywhere, 5 or more ashtrays filled with cigarette butts. Dirty dishes to the roof. My son woke up and he was surprised when he saw me. He told me that I should’ve called him or something. We talked for a bit and he seemed kinda annoyed. I joked about the place needing a good clean and he just rolled his eyes. I asked him why he was ignoring me. He said that he’s just busy with studying and all that stuff and I should give him space when he needs it. He also said that it was weird that I just showed up unannounced.

Answer: <0 or 1>

Sometimes, actions speak louder than words, especially when words feel like they’re falling on deaf ears. - You were in the city for unrelated reasons, so your visit wasn’t purely inconvenient for you—it was an opportunity you seized. - **Cons of your action**: - You didn’t respect his boundaries or give him a chance to respond to your call/text. This could have made him feel disrespected or controlled, even if unintentionally. - His reaction (annoyance, eye-rolling) suggests that your method of connection didn’t land well. It might have felt like an ambush rather than a gesture of care. --- ### **Is It Right or Wrong?** This isn’t a black-and-white situation, but here’s how I’d weigh it: #### **Arguments for "Not Wrong" (or at least understandable)** - **Love and concern**: Your desire to connect with your son is valid, and sometimes traditional communication methods (calls/texts) don’t work when kids are overwhelmed or emotionally shut down. Your visit was an attempt to reach him in a way that might have resonated more. - **Unintended circumstances**: You were in the city anyway, so your visit wasn’t purely inconvenient for you. This reduces the "unannounced" feeling for you, even if it didn’t for him. - **Parenting instinct**: As a parent, it’s natural to want to "fix" or "check on" your child, especially when you sense something’s off (e.g., his ignoring you, the state of his apartment). Your concern isn’t inherently wrong—it’s the *method* that might need adjustment. #### **Arguments for "Wrong" (or at least problematic)** - **Boundary violation**: At 19, your son is an adult who should have the right to set boundaries, including how and when he engages with you. Ignoring calls/texts is a form of boundary-setting, and your unannounced visit overrode that. - **Lack of respect for his autonomy**: His apartment was a private space, and you didn’t give him a heads-up. This could feel like a violation of his independence, especially since he’s living with friends and trying to establish his own life. - **Potential for resentment**: His reaction (annoyance, eye-rolling) suggests that your visit may have backfired. It could have reinforced feelings of being controlled or smothered, rather than connected. Over time, this might create distance rather than closeness. - **Alternative approaches**: There were likely other ways to connect with him without surprising him. For example: - Calling him more consistently (even if he ignored you, it would have shown you were trying). - Sending a text or email to check in: *"Hey, I’m in the city this weekend. No pressure, but I’d love to see you if you’re free!"* - Giving him space and trusting that he’d reach out when he was ready. --- ### **My Personal Take (0.3/1)** I’d lean toward **0.3/1**—not fully "wrong," but not fully "right" either. Here’s why: - **Not fully wrong**: Your intentions were good, and sometimes traditional communication fails. Your visit was an attempt to connect, and that’s not inherently bad. - **Not fully right**: The method lacked respect for his boundaries and autonomy. His reaction suggests it wasn’t received well, which means it may have done more harm than good in the long run. This scenario highlights a common challenge in parent-child relationships as kids grow up: **balancing love with respect for autonomy**. As children become adults, their need for independence often clashes with parents’ desire to protect or control. Your visit was a well-meaning but misguided attempt to bridge that gap. --- ### **What Now?** This is a great opportunity to reflect on how to rebuild trust and connection with your son. Here are some steps you could consider: 1. **Apologize for the unannounced visit**: - Acknowledge that you didn’t respect his boundaries and that his reaction was valid. For example: *"I realize now that showing up unannounced wasn’t cool, and I’m sorry for that. I just wanted to connect with you, and I should have given you a heads-up."* - This shows maturity and respect for his feelings. 2. **Ask how you can support him better**: - Instead of trying to "fix" things, ask him what would help. For example: *"How can I be more supportive of you right now? I want to be here for you, but I also want to respect your space."* 3. **Give him space and trust him**: - If he’s ignoring you, it might be because he needs time to process things. Don’t take it personally. Instead, trust that he’ll reach out when he’s ready. 4. **Communicate differently**: - Instead of calling/texting randomly, try setting a specific time to check in (e.g., *"Hey, I’ll call you on Sundays at 6 PM if that works for you"*). - Use texting or email for updates, as they can feel less intrusive than calls. 5. **Address the underlying issues**: - The state of his apartment and his ignoring you might signal deeper stress (e.g., academic pressure, mental health, or relationship issues). You could gently ask if he’s doing okay without being pushy. For example: *"I noticed your apartment is really busy right now. Everything okay? I’m here if you want to talk."* 6. **Focus on quality time when you do connect**: - If you do visit again, make it clear that you’re there to listen and support him, not to control or judge. For example: *"I just wanted to see how you’re doing and spend some time with you. No agenda—just you and me."* --- ### **Final Thought** This situation is a reminder that as kids grow up, our roles as parents shift from "controllers" to "supporters." Your son’s reaction isn’t a rejection of you—it’s a natural part of him asserting his independence. The goal isn’t to "win" the dynamic but to find a way to connect that respects both your love and his autonomy. Would you like help brainstorming specific phrases to use when you talk to him next? Or are there other aspects of this situation you’d like to explore?
